recruiting_oncology.title: Enhanced Ethanol Ablation for Feline Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
recruiting_oncology.description: Some cancer patients have a poor prognosis, despite intensive multimodal therapy (e.g., surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy). In other cases, these treatments are likely to improve outcome but are inaccessible (e.g., financial, scheduling and/or geographical limitations). Thus, there is an immense need for treatments that offer effective tumor control and palliation, and that ideally can be given at low-cost in the primary care setting. We have recently demonstrated proof-of-concept for a low-cost effective option, called enhanced ethanol ablation. Ethanol ablation (intratumoral injectionof pure ethanol) was originally used for human liver cancer, achieving survival rates similar to surgical resection for small tumors. However, conventional ethanol ablation is ineffective for superficial, large, and/or poorly encapsulated lesions, and requires large injection volumes. Enhanced ethanol ablation involves controlled injection of an ethyl cellulose- ethanol mixture directly into the tumor. When mixed with ethyl cellulose, a water-insoluble ethanol-based gel is formed. recruiting_oncology.title: Ethos Precision Medicine Umbrella Study for Hemangiosarcoma (Ethos-PUSH)
recruiting_oncology.description: Canine splenic hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive cancer with limited treatment options available. Dogs presenting with this disease often have spontaneous internal bleeding that results in sudden onset of weakness or collapse. Although this is a common consequence for hemangiosarcoma, any other tumor of the spleen can spontaneously bleed resulting in these same changes. Dogs who have a bleeding splenic tumor must undergo surgery to remove the spleen (called splenectomy). This procedure both removes the source of life-threatening hemorrhage and provides tissue samples for making a final diagnosis. Roughly 40% of dogs have benign splenic disease causing the internal bleeding and will be cured with surgery alone. Many of the remaining dogs will have hemangiosarcoma as the cause of their bleeding and will require chemotherapy following surgery to delay or prevent metastatic disease. For dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma, the combination of surgery and chemotherapy has been estimated to provide median survival times of 4-9 months with only a small percentage of dogs surviving to 2 years. recruiting_oncology.title: Minimally Invasive Metastasectomy in Canines (MIMIC) Trial
recruiting_oncology.description: Following surgical removal of the primary tumor and treatment with chemotherapy, the spread of cancer to the lungs (metastasis) is the most common cause of mortality in dogs with many tumors. A distinctive feature of lung metastases in human patients is the surprising benefit that can result from surgical removal of the lung metastases. The use of surgery to manage lung metastases in dogs has been described but is not commonly used due to the presumed post-surgical complications associated with conventional open chest surgery (thoracotomy). Innovations in minimally invasive surgery have created a new opportunity to include surgical removal of lung metastases with a reduced potential of complications when compared to the conventional thoracotomy techniques. Conventional thoracotomy techniques can be replaced by thoracoscopy, a surgical technique using miniature incisions in the chest to allow for removal of lung metastases with the assistance of a magnified video camera. This approach has the potential to significantly minimize the pain, potential complications, and recovery time in patients compared to what is observed with conventional thoracotomy techniques. recruiting_oncology.title: Vaccine Study for Dogs with Melanoma
recruiting_oncology.description: Participation involves an initial staging visit and 5 follow up visits. The vaccine will be given 4 times approximately 4 weeks apart followed by 2 restaging visits. Booster vaccines will also be available 6 months after completion of the entire vaccine series at an additional charge.

recruiting_oncology.title: Efficacy and safety of a novel anti-cancer therapeutic for the treatment of metastatic mammary carcinoma in cats

tags.label: Genetic (gene transfer, stem cell, recombinant DNA

recruiting_oncology.description: Purpose of Study:Mammary tumors are a commonly encountered cancer in cats, particularly in females, with 80-90% of masses diagnosed as malignant (carcinoma). Mammary carcinoma in cats parallels breast cancer in humans with regards to receptor expression profile and propensity of metastasis. The median survival time in cats ranges from 6 months to several years, depending on tumor size and grade. Greater than 60% of cats have more than one tumor at diagnosis, with the majority being high grade. The objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel therapeutic targeting miR-10b, a molecule responsible for viability of metastatic cells in cats with mammary carcinoma. This multipurpose therapy has a previously demonstrated efficacy in halting breast cancer invasion and metastasis in mice. The advantage of our novel therapeutic over existing drugs is that it can also be used to visualize primary and metastatic lesions in vivo by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Studies in cats with mammary carcinoma will help bring this therapeutic into clinic to treat human breast cancer.

recruiting_oncology.title: CAR T Cell and Verdinexor Therapy for Treatment of Glioma Tumors in Dogs
recruiting_oncology.description:
About the study


Every year, about 3 out of every 100 dogs will be diagnosed with a brain tumor. Many of these dogs will be diagnosed with a glioma tumor, which is the second most common type of brain tumor and also, unfortunately, the most difficult to treat. One of the most promising developing areas of research for treating glioma tumors is immunotherapy, which is a type of intervention that uses the dog's own cells to fight the cancer cells.


This study is looking at a specific type of immunotherapy called CAR T cell therapy. CAR T cells are created by doing a simple blood draw from the dog to extract the T cells ("fighter" cells), which are then infused with a Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) protein. This "upgrade" allows the T cells to target and attack the glioma tumor cells. This intervention has been used in children with brain tumors but this study will be the first time it's being used in dogs with glioma tumors!

recruiting_oncology.title: PSMA Ligand Based Theranostic to Treat Canine Prostatic Cancer
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Dr. David Holt, BVSc, Professor of Surgery, Diplomate (ACVS)
recruiting_oncology.description:
In this study, we will test a new research medication that combines a chemotherapy drug called MMAE (monomethyl Auristatin E) and a light-sensitive drug (Pc-413) and a laser light source (photodynamic therapy) to kill cancer cells in the prostate and in other areas of the body (metastatic disease). These two agents are linked to a molecule that binds to PSMA (prostate specific membrane antigen), a cell surface marker that is produced by prostatic cancer in large quantities. The research medication is inactive until it binds to PSMA. When the research medication binds to PSMA it is taken into the cell and activated. This means the research medication is targeted specifically to prostate cancer cells. The overall goal is to use this new research medication that is specific to prostate cancer cells to kill the cancer.


This study will cover the specific study related diagnostics once your dog is enrolled:

• Chest X-rays

• Abdominal ultrasound

• Prostate aspirate

• Blood work (CBC and chemistry)

• Urinalysis

• Physical examination

recruiting_oncology.title: Treating Dogs With Glioma Using Radiation and Immunotherapy
recruiting_oncology.description:
Gliomas are aggressive primary brain tumors that pose significant therapeutic challenges in both human and veterinary medicine. In dogs, gliomas are characterized by locally invasive growth and poor overall survival, even with intervention. Brachycephalic breeds—particularly French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers—are disproportionately affected, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition that remains under investigation.

Current treatment strategies for canine glioma typically involve surgical resection when anatomically feasible, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. Radiotherapy may also be used as a standalone treatment, delivered through various approaches, including conventionally fractionated protocols or stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT). SRT offers the advantages of high precision, greater tissue sparing, and shorter treatment duration. Despite these interventions, the prognosis remains guarded, with median survival times often not exceeding 12 months.

recruiting_oncology.title: Evaluation of a combination of three drugs in dogs with hemangiosarcoma
recruiting_oncology.description: The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin or carboplatin and temozolomide with propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. The use of either doxorubicin or carboplatin alone as a treatment for hemangiosarcoma has been studied, and studies with propranolol (historically used to treat heart disease) have shown promise as an added treatment against hemangiosarcoma, however, survival times still remain quite low. We are hopeful that survival times can be further improved using a combination approach to treatment, with combination of both intravenous and oral treatments. Dogs with hemangiosarcoma of the spleen, liver, heart or intramuscular region will be considered for inclusion in this study.

recruiting_oncology.title: Radiation + Targeted Therapy for Bladder Cancer in Dogs
recruiting_oncology.description:
Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) is the most common form of bladder tumors in dogs. Fractionated radiation therapy is one of the most effective treatment options for this form of tumor, and is typically combined with chemotherapy and an NSAID medication. Lapatinib is a newer therapy that has been used as a single agent for the treatment of dogs with this form of bladder tumor. The goal of this trial is to see if the combination of radiation therapy and lapatinib will be safe and well tolerated in dogs with TCC.


If your dog participates in this study, they will receive oral lapatinib through the course of the approximately 4-month study, as well as oral NSAIDs. 5-7 days after starting these medications, they will also complete 15 daily (M-F) fractions of radiation therapy, which requires daily general anesthesia. Patients will get a urinary ultrasound at the beginning and end of the study, which may require sedation for some patients. They will also receive routine bloodwork throughout the course of the study, as well as blood collection at the beginning of radiation, end of radiation, and the conclusion of the study for study purposes.

recruiting_oncology.title: Characterization of Soft Tissue Sarcoma Microscopic Extension
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Hunter Piegols, DVM, DACS-SA, ACVS Fellow-Surgical Oncology
recruiting_oncology.description:
The goal of the study is to assess the microscopic extension of soft tissue sarcomas. The enrollment will be limited to dogs cytologically or histologically diagnosed soft tissue sarcomas that are undergoing a wide excision. Wide surgical excision, defined as three-centimeter lateral margins and of layer of fascia (dense tissue) deep to the mass, will be performed as the standard of care. While under general anesthesia and immediately prior to routine surgery, sterile tattoo ink will be used to mark specific margins around the tumor. All tattoo ink will be within the tumor sample and planned margin with no tattoo ink applied outside the tissue to be removed.


There are no additional costs associated with the study beyond those acquired through routine care for the underlying condition. The study provides only costs toward the surgical procedure (mass removal) itself and the histopathology (biopsy) charges. This combination of charges would typically be $441-$1074 depending on tumor size. All other costs are the responsibility of the owner.

recruiting_oncology.title: Finding draining lymph nodes for anal gland tumors in dogs using minimally invasive surgery
recruiting_oncology.description: Anal sac cancers in dogs often spread to other areas of the body. This is called metastasis. Local lymph nodes are a common site for the cancer to spread in dogs with anal sac tumors. Removing lymph nodes with cancer improves outcome. However, assessment of the lymph nodes that drain fluid from a tumor can be challenging. A safe and common test is sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping. This is where we test the first lymph node(s) that drain fluid from a tumor for cancer cells. It has been used in dogs with anal sac cancer. However, the lymph nodes that drain anal sac tumors are located within the abdomen and pelvis. So far SLN mapping on dogs with anal sac tumors has needed open abdominal surgery. Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has many reported benefits for patients compared to open abdominal surgery, including smaller incisions, reduced pain, and earlier return to function. This is where small incisions are made for cameras and instruments, and tissue can be removed without making a large incision. recruiting_oncology.investigator: David Michael Vail, DVM, MS, DACVIM (Oncology), Professor
recruiting_oncology.description:

recruiting_oncology.title: Clinical Trial of Trametinib in Dogs with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)
recruiting_oncology.description:
Dogs can develop a serious blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This disease often gets worse quickly, and there is no standard treatment that reliably helps dogs live longer.

This study is testing a drug called trametinib to see if it may help dogs with AML. Trametinib is a medication used in people to treat some cancers. It works by blocking signals that help cancer cells grow. This drug is experimental for use in dogs with AML, and its safety and effectiveness for this condition are not yet known. In this study, all dogs will receive trametinib along with prednisone, which is commonly used to help dogs with leukemia feel better. About 13 dogs are expected to take part in this study.


Treatment is done with your local oncologist. As part of this study, pets will have the following things done:

• A physical exam by a veterinarian

• Blood tests to check blood counts and organ health

• Urine tests

• A cheek (buccal) swab to collect DNA for future research studies related to leukemia and treatment response

• Regular follow-up visits approximately 1 week and 2 weeks after starting treatment, approximately every 2 week

recruiting_oncology.title: Osteosarcoma- Targeted Bone Electrochemotherapy with Cementoplasty; Alternative to Amputation
recruiting_oncology.description:
Canine appendicular osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs. Standard treatment is amputation and chemotherapy with median survival around 13 months. Some patients are not candidates for amputation due to obesity, orthopedic conditions or other mitigating circumstances. Limb sparing is another option but limited in availability and is considered invasive.


Targeted bone electrochemotherapy (ECT-B) is an emerging focused cancer treatment therapy predominantly utilized in people with metastatic cancer to bone as a component of reducing bone pain and retarding tumor growth. It involves the insertion of a single pole electrode into the tumor and drawing chemotherapy directly to the tumor. In addition, once treatment is rendered, the remaining bone defect will be filled via sterile orthopedic bone cement, the patient recovered and discharged the same day.

recruiting_oncology.title: Developing a Blood Test for Early Detection of Bone Cancer Relapse
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Dr. Geoffrey Wood, DVM, PhD, DVSc Geoffrey Wood
recruiting_oncology.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone cancer in dogs, specially in large size breeds and it presents a high biological aggressiveness, in many cases at the time of diagnosis, metastatic dissemination has already occurred. Currently, the standard of care consists of surgical excision of the affected limb, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. However, despite initial therapeutic response, patients develop treatment resistance, leading to the presence of metastasis, most commonly within the lungs, reducing life expectancy and quality of life of the patient. 

Recently the use of liquid biopsies, a minimally invasive sample collection from body fluids, such as blood, has been increasing, as they detect specific molecular biomarkers. Liquid biopsies can aid in the detection of certain pathologies, monitor disease progression or recurrence after the treatment, the latter can be achieved by measuring molecules such as proteins and microRNAs that are in the circulating blood. These proteins and microRNA might provide less invasive and faster detection than other techniques, such as computerized tomography (CT scan).

recruiting_oncology.title: Using a Fluorescent Dye to Identify Bladder Tumors in Dogs During Surgery
recruiting_oncology.description:
Urothelial carcinoma (UC) is the most common type of bladder cancer in dogs. For dogs with tumors in certain locations, surgical removal (partial cystectomy) can improve outcomes with low risk. New minimally invasive techniques that maintain a closed bladder may offer additional benefits and warrant further investigation, but these approaches currently rely on specialized camera equipment within the bladder, which is not always available, to identify tumors. This pilot study will test whether a safe dye, indocyanine green (ICG), used with near-infrared (NIR) imaging can identify bladder tumors and their edges during surgery. The findings with NIR will be compared with what is seen by the surgeon and with microscopic examination by a pathologist. Results will be incorporated into future studies with novel surgical techniques that have the potential to improve outcomes in dogs with UC.

recruiting_oncology.title: CARE Trial: Combined Autophagy inhibition and Radiation therapy to improve Efficacy in Canine Glioma
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Christine Toedebusch, DVM, PhD, DACVIM, Associate Professor
recruiting_oncology.description:
Dogs diagnosed with glioma, an aggressive brain tumor, often experience limited benefit from standard treatments such as radiation therapy alone. This clinical trial is evaluating a novel investigational drug called bisaminoquinoline-13 (BAQ-13) that may help improve how brain tumors respond to radiation therapy.


BAQ-13 works by blocking a process called autophagy, which cancer cells use to survive treatment. This study will evaluate whether BAQ-13 can safely reach brain tumors, be tolerated by dogs receiving radiation therapy, and show early signs of effectiveness.


What happens in this study

  1. An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical and neurologic examination, blood work, and diagnostic imaging


  1. Advanced brain imaging (MRI and CT scans) performed under general anesthesia

recruiting_oncology.title: FLASH-Based Radioimmunotherapy in Canine Glioma
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Dr. Thomas Lee, DVM, DACVR, Radiation Oncologist
recruiting_oncology.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of FLASH proton radiation therapy (FLASH-RT), administered either alone or in combination with Gilvetmab, as a treatment for canine brain tumors (gliomas), with the goal of providing effective tumor control while reducing treatment-related side effects. FLASH-RT, combined with Gilvetmab, is considered experimental.


This trial offers three doses of FLASH-RT targeted for canine glioma with randomization to also receive three infusions of Gilvetmab following the RT protocol.


The three radiation therapy treatments happen on separate visits - usually Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. They are performed using standard of care general anesthesia. 


FLASH-RT: FLASH-RT treatments are performed at the Smilow Translational Research Building (STRB) in the evenings. This is a separate building a few blocks away from the veterinary hospital. Your dog will be transported to this building along with the study personnel, usually between 5-8 PM. Your dog will be anesthetized for the FLASH-RT treatments. Treatment has been limited to external beam radiation therapy at significant expense and often multiple days of anesthesia needed. Median survival is about 1 year and side effects are common. Electrochemotherapy is the use of electrical impulses to open cell membranes driving chemotherapy locally, i.e. a targeted therapy.

recruiting_oncology.title: The Effect of Intravenous Carboplatin on Pain Control in Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma
recruiting_oncology.description:
This study is currently on hold to enrollment due to a national shortage of carboplatin


We know from people and dogs with this type of bone cancer, that the pain associated with the tumor is severe. In people, after they receive their first round of chemotherapy, there is a significant reduction in the pain severity and of course an improvement in quality of life while undergoing treatment. A very important component of treatment in dogs, is ensuring effective pain control. What we dont know is the impact of adding chemotherapy to the pain control plan. This will help us inform current recommendations and the design of future clinical trials. The goal of this study is to determine the effect on lameness, activity and sleep quality in dogs with long bone osteosarcoma after a dose of intravenous carboplatin. Once enrolled, your dog will get a single dose of carboplatin chemotherapy, which is the standard of care drug we use in this disease. recruiting_oncology.title: CHOP vs. LOPP chemotherapy as a first line treatment for naïve peripheral T cell lymphoma in dogs
recruiting_oncology.description: Lymphoma comprises approximately 25% of all canine cancers. Up to 40% of these cases are caused by T lymphocytes, known as peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL). The vast majority of lymphoma cases cannot be addressed with surgery and instead warrant chemotherapy. The standard of care chemotherapy protocol for lymphoma is abbreviated CHOP, which stands for the 4 drugs involved. Generally, dogs with PTCL treated with CHOP chemotherapy tend to experience shorter remission durations and overall survival than dogs with diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL). When treated with CHOP chemotherapy, PTCL dogs have a median survival time of 4-9 months while DLBCL dogs have a median survival time of 11-13 months. Previous studies have questioned whether other, non-CHOP protocols may be better suited for dogs with PTCL in hopes of increasing remission and survival times. One protocol that has been repeatedly investigated is LOPP chemotherapy. This protocol uses two of the same drugs as CHOP and two that are different. Recent studies have demonstrated with dogs with PTCL treated with LOPP can experience survival times closer to 11-17 months. While these findings are promising, none of these inves

recruiting_oncology.title: Vaccine Study for Dogs with Splenic Hemangiosarcoma

tags.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

recruiting_oncology.description: The enrolled dogs will undergo removal of the spleen, followed by standard care therapy in addition to the vaccine. The vaccine will be given over 6 visits approximately 3 weeks apart in addition to 6 chemotherapy visits. If appropriate, your dog will also receive boosters every 6 months. The chemotherapy visits will be scheduled 2 weeks prior to each vaccine visit. At each visit, blood will also be drawn to measure the immune response for study purposes.

recruiting_oncology.title: Pilot study of Frunevetmab (Solensia) and Meloxicam for palliative therapy of feline bone-invasive oral squamous cell carcinomas
recruiting_oncology.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinomas are a common oral cancer in cats. These tumors are locally aggressive and associated with tissue and 
bone destruction. The average survival time of cats with this oral tumor type is reported to be 3 months or less, even after
aggressive treatment. Many owners elect to pursue palliative (pain relief) care options rather than cancer treatments. However, 
there can be challenges with palliative care as the selection of pain medication for cats is limited and most require oral
administration. There is an unmet need for pain medications that are safe and effective at maintaining a good quality of life for
cats with oral tumors. Therefore, the goal of this study is to evaluate a currently available injectable drug, which is marketed for the treatment of arthritis pain in cats, for its ability to also provide relief of pain associated with oral cancers.

recruiting_oncology.title: Pilot study evaluating palbociclib in dogs with melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, mammary carcinoma, or anal sac adenocarcinoma
recruiting_oncology.description: This is a clinical trial evaluating the use of a new chemotherapy drug, palbociclib, in tumor-bearing drugs with certain cancers. Palbociclib is currently used in humans with breast cancer and other tumors. It has been given to laboratory dogs to report some pharmacokinetic and toxicity data in preclinical trials. The intent of the clinical trial is to measure drug levels in dogs with cancer to determine a recommended prescription dose. We will also describe side effects and, while not a primary endpoint of the study, tumor response.

recruiting_oncology.title: Comparative Molecular Analysis for Acquired Toceranib Resistance in Dogs with Mast Cell Tumors
recruiting_oncology.description: The University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine is currently recruiting dogs diagnosed with non-resectable cutaneous Mast Cell Tumors (cMCTs) for a clinical research study. The purpose of this trial is to investigate novel biological characteristics associated with toceranib phosphate (Palladia®) resistance in canine cutaneous Mast Cell Tumors (cMCTs).

recruiting_oncology.title: Trametinib for Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Marilia Takada, DVM, MSc, PhD, DACVR
recruiting_oncology.description: The purpose of this research is to investigate a new anti-cancer drug, trametinib, that specifically ‘targets’ growth signals found in cancer cells from companion (pet) dogs. This study will determine the anti-tumor efficacy of trametinib in dogs with histiocytic sarcoma. We will measure and document how much the cancer shrinks upon treatment, and how the drug helps improve the patients’ outcome and life expectancy. Additionally, the study will test whether markers in the genes within the tumor can predict the response from treatment, which in the future can help select those dogs that are more likely to respond positively to treatment. Finally, in a simple blood test we will determine whether effective drug levels are present in the patient.

recruiting_oncology.title: Incidence of hypercoagulability and thromboembolism in dogs with surgically treated primary hepatocellular and adrenal neoplasia
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Laura Selmic, MPH, DACVS-SA, DECVS, Surgical Oncology
recruiting_oncology.description:
The goal of this study is to characterize the hemostatic abnormalities in dogs with primary hepatocellular or primary adrenal cancer undergoing surgical removal and to determine when their hypercoagulability (increased tendency for blood to clot) resolves post-operatively. Additionally, we aim to determine the incidence of thromboembolism (blood clots) in hypercoagulable patients diagnosed with primary hepatocellular or primary adrenal cancer following tumor removal.


Dogs with suspected primary hepatocellular or adrenal neoplasia will undergo standard-of-care procedures, including blood work (CBC, chemistry, and PT/PTT) and CT of the abdomen. Upon enrollment, a TEG and fibrinogen level will be obtained before surgery for the study. Dogs will return in 10-14 days for re-check full-body CT and blood work (PCV/TS, TEG, PLT, fibrinogen). Dogs will return in 15-21 days for re-check blood work. Dogs will continue to return for recheck blood work (PCV/TS, TEG, fibrinogen, and PLT) until their hypercoagulability, based on an elevated TEG G-value, resolves.

recruiting_oncology.title: CAR T cell Immunotherapy for Treatment of Metastatic Osteosarcoma in Dogs
recruiting_oncology.description: Osteosarcoma (OS) is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that have macroscopic metastases to the lungs. CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) T cells are a modified version of a T cell, a type of immune cell, that alters them so they can target and destroy cancer cells. Dogs have been previously treated with CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) T cells at other institutions and the treatment has been well-tolerated, but the new CAR T cells being evaluated in this trial have not been evaluated in dogs with cancer, though safety studies were done in healthy dogs, without side effects. The goal of this study is to determine the safety and effectiveness of canine CAR T cells, which will be generated by gene modification of your dogs white blood cells, and then infused back into your dog by an intravenous catheter. In order to help the CAR T cells expand in the body more effectively, your dog will also have to be treated with bone marrow suppressing drugs (fludarabine and cyclophosphamide) for 2 days before the CAR T cells are given b

recruiting_oncology.title: Clinical Testing of Canine T cells Engineered to Target Osteosarcoma and Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Combination with Oral Immunotherapy
recruiting_oncology.description: The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the safety and anti-cancer activity of fibroblast activation protein (FAP) targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, alone or in combination with orally administered immunotherapy drugs, in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. FAP is a protein that is expressed on the surface of tumor cell and can be recognized by a T cell. CAR T cells are when a patient’s own cancer fighting white blood cells are modified to express a receptor which binds a specific molecule expressed on the surface of a tumor cell. The two oral immunotherapy drugs being used in combination with FAP CAR T cells (losartan and toceranib [Palladia]) have already been extensively evaluated in a prior trial in dogs with bone cancer and have demonstrated considerable anti-cancer activity, with minimal toxicity. Studies in rodent models of cancer and in vitro in human and canine OS cell lines have indicated that FAP CAR T cells can exert robust killing of canine OS cells and may complement the activities of toceranib and losartan. recruiting_oncology.title: Canine Liver Tumor Study
recruiting_oncology.description:
North Carolina State University College of Veterinary Medicine is currently enrolling canine patients that have 1-2 liver tumors into a clinical trial that is using a new therapy called INSPIRE, which uses electrical pulses to safely destroy the cells within a tumor.


This study has two treatment group:


One group of study applicants should have 1-2 liver tumors measuring between 1-3cm. Potential candidates will come in through the Medical Oncology service at NC State Veterinary hospital for a screening appointment to check eligibility for enrollment. If the patient is eligible for the study and their tumors are eligible for surgical resection, the patients in this group will return one week later for a one time INSPIRE treatment followed by liver lobectomy a week later to remove the tumors.


The second group of study applicants should have 1-2 liver tumors measuring between 1-3cm. Potential candidates will come in through the Medical Oncology service at NC State Veterinary Hospital for a screening appointment to check eligibility for enrollment. recruiting_oncology.investigator: Dr. J. Impellizeri DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), MRCVS, CMO

recruiting_oncology.description:
Metastatic disease prevents a unique clinical setting especially when the patients is still stable. Options are limited for treatment but may include oral and IV chemotherapy options. With the advent of PD-1 inhibitors, we are now looking to combine the inhibitor with either Telomerase or HER2 immunotherapy in combination as the combined therapies should improve response while minimizing adverse effects and battling the cancer through specific mechanisms.

Inhibitors of the immune checkpoint proteins cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen (CTLA)-4, programmed death (PD)-1, and PD ligand 1 (PD-L1) can induce durable remissions in a subset of patients with metastatic disease. However, these treatments can be limited by inflammatory toxicities that can affect any orga

recruiting_oncology.title: Immunotherapy for canine oral melanoma
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Shay Bracha, DVM, DACVIM, Associate Professor
recruiting_oncology.description:
Oral melanoma is a highly aggressive disease with poor outcomes and no effective treatments. Our recent research has shown that a weakened form of the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is safe, and can trigger strong anti-tumor effects.


By injecting a small amount of this weakened virus directly into the tumor, we aim to activate the dog's immune system to fight the cancer. Additionally, we will collect and expand immune cells from the tumor, as these cells are more likely to recognize and attack cancer cells. These enhanced immune cells will then be reinfused into the patient to target existing or potential metastatic disease.


To evaluate our therapy, we will first perform a tumor biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and analyze the immune cells already present (Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes). We will then inject the tumor with the weakened virus. One week later, the tumor will be surgically removed, and immune cells from the cancer will be expanded for future use if metastases are present or develop later. After treatment, we will closely monitor the patients through periodic blood tests and imaging (CT scans) every three months.

recruiting_oncology.title: COSMyc- IT Trial- Canine Oncology Study for Myc Inhibition Tolerability Trial
recruiting_oncology.description:
Myc (a family of transcription factors encompassing c-, N-, and L-Myc) is a pleiotropic, evolutionarily conserved transcription factor. Myc is one of the most frequently amplified oncogenes in most (perhaps all) human cancers (Dang 2012, Whitfield 2017) and often correlates with aggressiveness of the disease (Wolfer 2010; Lee 2015). In breast cancer, Myc is overexpressed in 30–50% of high-grade tumors, is markedly elevated in triple-negative breast cancer and even further elevated in tumors that display a drug-resistant phenotype (Fallah 2017). In non-small cell lung cancer, Myc amplification is found in up to 30% of malignancies (Ahmadzada 2018; Kalkat 2017).


A new novel peptide that inactivates Myc has been developed and is currently in human trials. The goal of this study is to determine the tolerability and feasibility of administering this novel peptide to dogs with cancer to inform future efficacy studies.

recruiting_oncology.title: Radiotherapy Trial for Metastatic Bone Cancer in Dogs
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Dara Kraitchman, VMD, PhD, Professor and Director
recruiting_oncology.description:
Purpose of the study: 

This study seeks to determine whether a new treatment can be safe and effective to stop osteosarcoma or bone cancer that has spread or metastasized beyond the tumor in the limb.  Your pet will receive a small amount of a radiotherapy, which consists of a radioactive compound linked to a monoclonal antibody, called “225-Actinium 3F8 (225Ac-3F8) in a vein. We will then do a specialized type of imaging called Single Photo Emission Computed Tomography(SPECT) combined with a computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan to determine whether your pet’s tumor takes up this agent. We will also take samples of blood, urine, and feces to try and determine the maximum dose that your dog can tolerate. We may then give an additional dose of 225Ac-3F8 in a vein several days later to treat your dog. We will follow-up with sampling of the blood and another specialized imaging called Positron Emission Tomography-Computed Tomography (PET-CT) at approximately 40 days after treatment to determine your dog's response.

recruiting_oncology.title: Enrolling Dogs with Invasive Bladder Cancer
recruiting_oncology.description: NC State Medical Oncology is enrolling patients for a clinical trial of an experimental immunotherapy for the treatment of bladder cancer. The primary purpose of this study is to investigate the safety and immune-stimulating properties of a novel therapy being developed at NCSU.

recruiting_oncology.title: Combination chemotherapy (Doxorubicin-Temozolomide with or without propranolol) in dogs with Hemangiosarcoma
recruiting_oncology.description: The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin and temozolomide with or without propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. The use of either doxorubicin alone as a treatment for hemangiosarcoma has been studied, and studies with propranolol (historically used to treat heart disease) have shown promise as an added treatment against hemangiosarcoma, however, survival times still remain quite low. A sister drug to Temozolomide, DTIC, has shown promise in improving survival times, however side effects and the long administration times have created challenges with the use of DTIC in dogs. Temozolomide is administered orally and is historically well tolerated in dogs. We are hopeful that survival times can be further improved using a combination approach to treatment, with combination of both intravenous and oral treatments and improved tolerability. Dogs with hemangiosarcoma of the spleen, liver, heart or intramuscular region will be considered for inclusion in this study.

recruiting_oncology.title: Combinatorial Imaging with PDL1-IRDye800 to Guide Surgical Treatment of Oral Cancer
recruiting_oncology.description:
Background and purpose


For dogs diagnosed with oral cancer (Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Oral Malignant Melanoma), curative intent surgical removal has been consistently found to have the longest remission rate. However, conventional diagnostic imaging, which we use to plan our surgery, is imperfect and can underestimate the extent of the tumor which results in the potential that not all cancer cells are removed during surgery. This directly impacts patient outcomes (disease free interval and overall survival). There is a critical need to improve our ability to detect cancer intraoperatively (i.e. during the surgery) to improve patient outcomes.


Further, for human head and neck cancer the standard of care is to give immunotherapy (drugs that improve the immune system's ability to fight off cancer) prior to surgery, which has resulted in increased survival in a subset of patients. We have no data on this type of pre-surgical treatment in dogs, and if it would also improve patient survival times.

recruiting_oncology.title: Pilot Study for a New Quasiorganelle Therapy in Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma
recruiting_oncology.description:
Histiocytic sarcoma is an aggressive cancer in dogs that often does not respond well to standard treatments like chemotherapy or radiation. While some dogs experience benefits, these treatments affect many cells at once and cannot adapt as a tumor changes. New research shows that cancer closely interacts with the immune system and surrounding tissues, suggesting that better treatments may need to work inside cells, not just target them from the outside. Quasiorganelle therapy is an experimental approach that aims to do this by using weakened, non-disease-causing bacteria derived from Listeria monocytogenes to deliver helpful genetic instructions directly into immune and tumor cells, with the goal of improving how the body recognizes and responds to cancer.


The first group (8 dogs) will receive quasiorganelle therapy alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the quasiorganelle infusion. They will then be observed for up 4 days at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center and blood and fecal samples will be taken at set timepoints. recruiting_oncology.title: Treatment of Canine Sarcoma with FAP CAR T-cells (FAP CAR-T Study)
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Rachel Brady, DVM, PhD, Assistant Professor
recruiting_oncology.description:
CAR T cell therapy has fundamentally changed how certain cancers are treated. By reprogramming a patient's own T lymphocytes to express a receptor targeting a protein on tumor cells, it directs the immune system to destroy them, producing durable remissions in blood cancers once refractory to conventional treatment.


These benefits have yet to reach veterinary patients, and some cancers remain especially hard to treat with immunotherapy. Sarcomas can be very resistant to standard treatment across many species, including dogs. Led by investigators at Colorado State University, we are testing CAR T cells engineered against FAP, a protein highly expressed in many sarcomas, in pet dogs. We are evaluating both the therapy's activity and its side effects. Advancing this work meets a real clinical need for companion animals while accelerating progress for human patients as well.


In this study, we will test a new treatment for dogs with sarcomas. As the tumor has to be biopsied, this study is best for sarcomas that are external or on the outside of the body.

recruiting_oncology.title: Targeted Electrochemotherapy (ECT) Cancer Treatment
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Dr. J Impellizeri, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), MRCVS, CMO
recruiting_oncology.description:
Targeted Electrochemotherapy (ECT) treatment consists of delivering a low dose of chemotherapy, followed by short electric pulses to the cancer. With the delivery of the electric pulses, cell membranes are transiently opened allowing chemotherapy directly into the cell. Treatment may be repeated over the course of weeks or months to achieve regression of large lesions. Targeted Electrochemotherapy employs lower dosages of chemotherapeutic drugs than standard chemotherapy protocols. In the clinical use of electrochemotherapy, side effects are uncommon and patients maintain or improve quality of life. Currently, Electrochemotherapy in animals is under a short anesthesia and with a variety of electrodes available to us, many tumor types and locations (including internal cancers) are candidates for this therapy.


Targeted Electrochemotherapy, in veterinary oncology (dogs, cats, exotics and horses), has been dominated by centers in Europe and South America. Here at Veterinary Oncology Services, there is not a location where cancer may not be treated. It may be used for a wide variety of tumors including:

recruiting_oncology.title: Combination of electrochemotherapy and gene therapy with canine IL-12
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Dr. J. Impellizeri DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), MRCVS, CMO

recruiting_oncology.description:
Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is an advanced treatment in veterinary oncology. It has been routinely used in dogs for treating mast cell tumors, carcinomas and soft tissue sarcomas, in cats for SCC, carcinomas and sarcomas and in horses for sarcoid tumors. ECT is a local ablative technique which has a good local anti-tumor control in dogs (up to 70%) and in cats (up to 80%) and in horses up to 100% but limited impact on distant tumors and metastasis. Therefore, there is a need for a combination therapy which could provide local control with a systemic effect to battle cancer spread. Interleukin 12 is a potent immune stimulator that works by increasing IFN gamma which has an anti-tumor effects through the activation of cytotoxic cells such as natural killer cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes. IL-12 also up-regulates antigen presenting cells making the tumor cells recognizable to the immune system. Several clinical studies have already been performed treating different canine tumors by electro-genetransfer with a plasmid encoding IL-12. Results showed increased systemic IL-12 and IFN gamma with an effect on distant metastasis .

recruiting_oncology.title: Exploring a Nonoparticle-enabled Treatment of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Cats
recruiting_oncology.description:
For veterinary patients, surgery is the primary treatment for many tumour types. Surgery may not always be the best option for cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC) as it is challenging to obtain adequate clear surgical margins and often, the disease reoccurs. Adjuvant therapies including chemotherapy, radiation therapy and palliative options are ineffective or poorly tolerated and do not improve the overall survival rate of cats with OCSCC. We need to make improvements to staging and treatment.

PORPHYSOMES (pPs) are a novel nanomedicine developed and supplied by Professor Dr Gang Zheng’s Laboratory (University Health Network, Toronto). These particles are delivered intravenously (in a local vein through a catheter) and concentrate in areas with tumour cells (either the primary tumour location or where the cancer has spread (metastatic site). pPs can be used to highlight the tumour by using a specialized technique called near-infrared fluorescence imaging (NIRF). recruiting_oncology.title: Vaccine study for Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma
recruiting_oncology.description: The enrolled dogs will undergo amputation or radiation of the affected limb followed immediately by vaccination every 3 weeks. The vaccine will be given over 6 visits approximately 3 weeks apart in addition to 6 chemotherapy visits. If appropriate your dog will also receive boosters every 6 months after completing the initial series. The chemotherapy visits will be scheduled 2 weeks prior to each vaccine visit. At each visit, blood will also be drawn to measure the immune response for study purposes.

recruiting_oncology.title: Dual Energy CT to Assess Bone Mineral Density in Dogs with Osteosarcoma Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy
recruiting_oncology.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs and, while amputation followed by systemic chemotherapy is the standard of care, it may not be the most appropriate treatment option for all dogs or it may not meet the goals of individual owners. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) has been utilized to kill tumor cells while leaving the affected limb intact showing good primary tumor control rates. The biggest risk with using SBRT in this setting is the potential for pathologic fracture of the affected limb. Here we plan to use a dual energy CT for radiation planning and to quantify bone mineral density (BMD) both before and after SBRT to assess changes that happen with SBRT treatment. BMD measures calcium and other minerals. In theory, the more mineral, the denser and stronger the bone is and less likely it is to break. In addition, we will measure bone breakdown markers before and after treatment to determine how these are correlated with the BMD and response to treatment.

recruiting_oncology.title: Dose escalation study for a novel STING agonist in tumor-bearing dogs
recruiting_oncology.description:
Immunotherapy, engaging the power of the immune system against cancer, has become a standard part of oncology care. One such approach utilizes the STimulator of INterferon Genes (STING) pathway. Our colleagues at University of Michigan, led by Dr. James Moon, have developed a drug that activates the STING pathway. This drug, called CMP-002, has been shown to combat cancer in a laboratory setting, with and without the use of another modulator of immune system, PD-1 blockade. This success prompted a collaboration with Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine as we hope to contribute to efforts that can help veterinary oncology patients and humans alike. Our initial studies, led by Dr. Vilma Yuzbasiyan-Gurkan at MSU, established the dose range tolerated in healthy dogs.

The purpose of this study is to confirm the best dose of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade for tumor-bearing dogs. CMP-002 has already been tested in healthy dogs. It is not uncommon for patients with cancer to process drugs differently, which is why we intend to confirm the best dose for tumor-bearing dogs. The findings of this study will then be used in future studies assessing the anti-c

recruiting_oncology.title: Mammary tumors in cats
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Laura Selmic, MPH, DACVS-SA, DECVS, Surgical Oncology
recruiting_oncology.description:
Surgery is the most common treatment used for mammary cancer in cats. The pathologist determines whether surgery has removed all cancer cells many days after the procedure. We need rapid and accurate testing during surgery to detect residual cancer to decrease cancer recurrence and the necessity for repeated surgery or treatments.


Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technology that uses near-infrared light waves to generate real-time, high-resolution images of the microscopic structure of tissues, specifically looking at the organization of the tissues. We have performed some initial evaluations using this optical coherence tomography for detection of residual cancer, which has had very encouraging results.


Cats will undergo surgery to remove their tumor; following removal, the tumor will be scanned with polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography to assess the surgical margins for residual cancer cells. The specimen will then undergo thorough histopathological assessment.


The overall purpose of the study is to evaluate a new imaging method to detect cancer cells left behind followi

recruiting_oncology.title: Electrochemotherapy for Bone Cancer
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Dr. J. Impellizeri DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), MRCVS, CMO
recruiting_oncology.description:
Electrochemotherapy is a valuable anti-cancer therapy in both human and veterinary patients. Until recently, there was no electrode to allow treatment of bone lesions. Veterinary Oncology Services (www.petcancerinformation.com) has a bone electrode used in human applications (see below).

Bone metastases induce pain, risk of fracture, and neural compression, and reduced mobility and quality of life. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive local treatment based on a high-voltage electric pulse combined with an anticancer drug. recruiting_oncology.title: Immune treatment of Canine Bone Cancer
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Dara L Kraitchman, VMD, PhD, Professor of Radiology and Director CIGAT
recruiting_oncology.description: Dogs with bone cancer or osteosarcoma of the limbs will be first assessed with a specialized imaging called 18F-FDG PET-CT to determine that the tumor is limited to the leg. Once enrolled, the dog will be treated with an immunotherapy directly in the tumor followed by chemotherapy the next 1-2 days prior to amputation. The goal of this therapy is to increase the immune response to the tumor. After amputation, treatment with standard chemotherapy will be augmented with an immune checkpoint inhibitor. At three, six, and twelve months after amputation, non-invasive imaging will be performed to look for spread of osteosarcoma. All treatments performed at the Center for Image-Guided Animal Therapy at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, MD are free-of-charge. The immune checkpoint inhibitor will be provided free-of-charge. The owner will need to make arrangements for amputation and chemotherapy with a surgeon and medical oncologist, respectively.

recruiting_oncology.title: Feasibility and dose-optimization clinical trial of local immunotherapy for solid tumors in canine cancer patients
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Kristen Couto, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), Veterinary Oncologist
recruiting_oncology.description:
WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?

Immunotherapies are a class of anti-cancer treatments that work by activating a patient’s own immune system to fight specific diseases, including cancer. A number of immunotherapies have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in humans in a wide range of diseases, including cancer. While these therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells, they have had more limited successes in solid tumors like soft tissue sarcoma. This is thought to be in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing serious side effects. To overcome this limitation, this research study will use injections of immunotherapies directly through the skin into the tumor (intra-tumoral injections). 


The primary goal of this research study is to test whether it is safe and feasible to treat tumors by injecting them with a certain type of immunotherapy called T-cell engagers (TCEs).  A T cell is a special kind of white blood cell that attacks sick cells in your body, including virus-inf

recruiting_oncology.title: Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Kathryn Wolfert, DVM, Medical Oncology resident
recruiting_oncology.description:
Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas.


Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy.

recruiting_oncology.title: Novel Immunotherapy for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
recruiting_oncology.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a very difficult cancer to treat in cats and is often fairly advanced before it is detected. This clinical trial will be examining the effectiveness of a new type of immunotherapy for treating this disease in cats, which is based on very promising data from two squamous cell carcinoma trials conducted recently in horses at CSU. This new treatment is designed to stimulate the body’s own immune defenses to attack the tumor cells and cause tumor regression or elimination. In this particular trial, even stopping the tumor from growing (rather than full elimination) would be considered a success. This immunotherapy drug has been tested previously in cats, and is generally well-tolerated, with few side-effects, but it has only been evaluated in one cat with oral squamous cell carcinoma previously. The treatment has however been extensively evaluated in horses with squamous cell carcinoma, with a high degree of success. In this study, we will evaluate this novel immunotherapy in cats with oral SCC to determine how well the treatment works and how well it is tolerated by cats.

recruiting_oncology.title: PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma
recruiting_oncology.investigator: Christine Toedebusch, DVM, PhD, DACVIM, Associate Professor
recruiting_oncology.description:
High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.


The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.


Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.

recruiting_oncology.title: Radiation Treatment for Cats with Small Cell GI Lymphoma
recruiting_oncology.description:
Feline small cell gastrointestinal lymphoma (SCGL) is a common cancer in cats causing chronic weight loss, vomiting, and diarrhea. While standard effective treatments involve daily pills, not all cats will tolerate these medications. This study investigates a pill-free alternative with three daily radiation treatments (RT). To attempt to ensure the treatments are safe for the cats’ gastrointestinal tracts, a specialized delivery method that administers the radiation more slowly will be utilized. Cats with a diagnosis of SCGL who have experienced symptoms for more than six weeks and who have not yet received treatment can be enrolled. After radiation treatment, we will check how well the cats respond to treatment and watch for side effects. Additionally, we will test stool samples from the cats during the study to help us learn about the healthy and harmful bacteria in the cats’ intestines. The goal of this study is to find a treatment that is easy to complete, safe, helpful, and improves the quality of life for cats with SCGL.
